in_hebrew.name: תלסיה
in_hebrew.long_meaning: תלסיה נגזר מהמילה היוונית θάλασσα (תלאסה), שפירושה ים. השם תלסיה משויך לנצרות ומתאר אדם הקשור לים או לאוקיינוס, ויכול לסמל את העומק והרחבה של האמונה הנוצרית.

in_greek.name: Θαλαссия
in_greek.long_meaning: Η Θαλασία προέρχεται από την ελληνική λέξη θάλασσα, που σημαίνει θάλασσα ή ωκεανός. Στην παράδοση της Εκκλησίας, το όνομα Θαλασία συμβολίζει τη σχέση με τη θάλασσα της ζωής και την πνευματική αναζήτηση.

in_latin.name: Thalassia
in_latin.long_meaning: Thalassia derivatur a verbo Graeco θάλασσα, quod significat mare. Nomen Thalassia in traditione Christiana significat personam quae cum mari vel oceano coniungitur, et potest symbolum esse profunditatis et latitudinis fidei Christianae.

in_english.name: Thalassia
in_english.meaning: Of the sea, ocean, or marine
in_english.long_meaning: The name Thalassia originates from the Greek word θάλασσα (thalassa), meaning sea or ocean. In Christian tradition, Thalassia symbolizes a connection to the vastness and depth of the sea, reflecting spiritual growth and exploration. Historically, the name may relate to early Christian communities near the Mediterranean. The personality associated with Thalassia is often considered adventurous, profound, and spiritually inclined.

historical_references.reference: St. Thalassia of Calabria (also known as St. Thalassia of Sicily), was an early Christian martyr who lived during the 3rd or 4th century. According to legend, she was a virgin and a nun who lived near Miletus in Asia Minor. When the region was invaded by the Saracens, St. Thalassia went to Calabria, Italy, to escape persecution. She settled in Rossano and founded a monastery there. The Saracens eventually invaded Calabria and killed St. Thalassia, along with several other nuns, for refusing to renounce their faith. She is venerated as a patron saint of the Adriatic Sea and of Calabria.

A different St. Thalassia is mentioned in Greek hagiography from the 16th century. She was a nun from Constantinople who lived during the 9th or 10th century. According to legend, she was miraculously saved from a shipwreck in the Aegean Sea and then became a hermit on the island of Thasos. She is often depicted holding a cross and a book, and is believed to have performed many miracles during her lifetime. Her relics were transferred to the Monastery of St. John the Theologian in Crete in the 17th century.
